workEn: The Secret History of the Mongols
title: 元朝秘史 §§200–200
titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §200: Jamuqa brought before Chinggis
source: Mongγol-un niγuča tobčiyan (The Secret History of the Mongols), §§200–200, in the Ming Chinese-character phonetic transcription, as edited with a romanized reading by Shiratori Kurakichi 白鳥庫吉, 音訳蒙文元朝秘史 (Tokyo, 1943), itself based on the Ye Dehui 葉德輝 printed edition of 1905/1908; text taken from the Japanese Wikisource transcription, archived and verified against it character for character. Shiratori died in 1942, so the edition was public domain in Japan before the URAA date and was never restored in the United States. Section numbering (§) is the standard citation system. Romanization convention: Shiratori's, kept exactly as he prints it (γ, ġ, ṅ, ž, č, and the raised dot of γ̇). Translations are made fresh from the Mongolian, with the Ming interlinear Chinese glosses as the primary crib. No modern translation was consulted. langCode is null: there is no text-to-speech for Middle Mongol.
about: Section 200 gives the capture of Jamuqa. With his people taken from him, he is taken by his own five companions and brought to Chinggis; Chinggis has the companions beheaded before his eyes for laying hands on their lord, and offers Jamuqa a place at his side once more, reminding him of the services he once did. Jamuqa’s answer is not part of this section.
draftNote: The Mongol readings follow Shiratori throughout; the English is a first drafting.

sentences.t: Naiman Merkid-i muqudγan baraγ̇asu

morph.gloss: accusative: marks the object (the Ming 行) [種名行]
to impoverish, make poor (causative; stem inferred from the Ming) [敎窮]
to end, be finished; here an auxiliary, ‘once done’ [極呵]
conditional converb: if, when (back-vowel form) [極呵]

sentences.l: Naiman Merkid-(object) impoverishing, finished-when,
sentences.i: When the Naiman had finished impoverishing the Merkid,
sentences.n: The part opens mid-story, with a conditional clause in -γasu (“when, if”). muqudγan is read from the Ming 敎窮, “cause to be poor”: a causative stem muqudγa- (perhaps from muqu- “bad, poor”; the stem is inferred) with the converb -n. baraγ̇asu is bara- “end, be finished” as an auxiliary: “once it was done”. Merkid-i is the accusative (Ming 行), so the Naiman are the subject, not “Naiman and Merkid”.

sentences.t: Žamuqa Naiman- luγ̇a bürün tende ulus(i)-jan abdaγ̇asu

morph.gloss: comitative: with, together with (back-vowel form) [一同]
there, then (locative adverb from tere ‘that’) [那裏]
people, subjects (the (i) is Shiratori’s) [百姓 自的行]
reflexive-possessive: one’s own (back-vowel form) [百姓 自的行]
conditional converb: if, when (back-vowel form) [被要了呵]

sentences.l: Jamuqa Naiman with being, there own-people taken-when,
sentences.i: Jamuqa was with the Naiman, and when his own people had been taken there,
sentences.n: Note that Shiratori prints Naiman- and luγ̇a as two words (the Ming glosses them 種名 and 一同 separately), so the comitative is “Naiman with”. bürün is bü- “be” + the time-converb -rün (Ming 有的). abdaγ̇asu is ab- “take” + the passive -da- + -γ̇asu: “when (his people) had been taken” (Ming 被要了呵). ulus(i)-jan is “one’s own people”, the (i) being Shiratori’s. The text does not say who took them; the sense is that Jamuqa’s following was lost, which is why he has five companions next. This is the second -γasu clause in a row; the main verb waits for ügüležüġü, three units on.

sentences.t: mün tabun nöködtü oγ̇orčaγ bolžu

morph.gloss: the very, he himself (Ming 他 ‘he’; elsewhere ‘just, the very’; uncertain here) [他]

sentences.l: he-himself five companion-having, robber becoming,
sentences.i: he, with five companions, turned brigand,
sentences.n: nöködtü is nökör “companion” + the plural -d + -tü “having” (the possessive pattern again: “companion-having”, as in “wife-having”). oγ̇orčaγ is the Ming 刼, “robber, plunderer” (earlier parts gloss it 劫賊), and oγ̇orčaγ bolžu is “becoming a robber”. mün is glossed 他 “he” here; elsewhere it is “just, the very”, so “he himself” is my reading and an uncertain one; I leave it out of i.

sentences.t: Taṅlu deġere γarču uγulža alažu širažu iderün

morph.gloss: to go out, go up [上着]
converb: -ing (the form after a consonant, back-vowel) [上着]

sentences.l: Taṅlu on going-up, argali killing, roasting, eating-when,
sentences.i: went up onto Mount Tanglu, and while he killed and roasted argali and ate,
sentences.n: A converb chain: γarču (going up), alažu (killing), širažu (roasting), each in -žu/-ču “-ing”, running into iderün “when eating” (ide- “eat” + the time-converb -rün). I keep the chain in one unit and let the main verb arrive in the next. Taṅlu is a mountain (Ming 山名); I write it Tanglu. deġere is “on, above” (Ming 上). uγulža is the Ming 羱羊, a wild mountain sheep (argali). γarču is γar- “go out, go up” with the form -ču that follows a consonant stem.

sentences.t: tende Žamuqa nököd-teġen ügüležüġü.

morph.gloss: reflexive-possessive: one’s own [伴當每 (自的)行]
past narrative: spoke (front-vowel form of -žuγ̇u) [說了有]

sentences.l: there Jamuqa companions-his-own-to spoke.
sentences.i: Jamuqa then said to his own companions:
sentences.n: The main verb at last. nököd-teġen is nökör + the plural -d + the dative-locative -te + the reflexive -ġen, “to his own companions” (Ming 伴當每(自的)行); this is the reflexive pattern of the conventions (-beġen/-deġen/-jüġen), here with -ġen after the dative -te. ügüležüġü is ügüle- “say” with the narrative past -žüġü, the front-vowel form of -žuγ̇u. Shiratori ends the unit with a full stop where I read a colon, since the speech follows.

sentences.t: Ken-ü köġüd ene üdür uγulža alažu ein idemü" keġežüġü.
sentences.l: Whose sons this day argali killing thus eat? saying said.
sentences.i: “Whose sons are they who, this day, kill argali and eat like this?” he said.
sentences.n: Shiratori closes the quotation (idemü") but never opens it; I supply the opening mark in i. Ken-ü köġüd is “whose sons”, an exclamatory or rhetorical question rather than a request for names; I take it as a boast (“What sons they are!”) but only the grammar is certain, not the tone. idemü is ide- “eat” + the present -mü (Ming 喫有); keġežüġü is keġe- “say” + -žüġü, so “said”. The pair alažu … idemü is again converb + finite verb.

sentences.t: Tere uγulža-jin miqa iden büküi žaγ̇ura

morph.gloss: argali, wild mountain sheep [羱羊 的]
genitive: of (after a vowel) [羱羊 的]

sentences.l: That argali’s meat eating being, during,
sentences.i: While he was eating the meat of that argali,
sentences.n: uγulža-jin is the genitive (-jin after a vowel) of the argali, “of the argali”; tere is “that”, capitalised only because it opens a sentence. iden büküi is iden “eating” (converb) + büküi “being” (the participle of bü-), a progressive; žaγ̇ura is žaγ̇ur “midst, interval” + the dative-locative -a, so “during, in the midst of” (Ming 間).

sentences.t: tabun nököd in-ü Žamuqa-ji γardažu barižu Čiṅgis Qaγan-dur abčiražuγ̇u.

morph.gloss: his, her, its (third-person genitive, placed after its noun) [他的]
Jamuqa, a man's name [人名 行]
accusative: marks the object (after a vowel) [人名 行]
to lay a hand on, set hand to [下手着]
to seize, take hold of [拿着]
Chinggis, the title borne by Temüjin from 1206 [太祖︀]
to bring along (ab- ‘take’ + a form of ire- ‘come’; analysis uncertain) [將着來了有]
past narrative: brought (back-vowel form) [將着來了有]

sentences.l: five companions his Jamuqa-(object) hand-laying, seizing, Chinggis Qaγan-to brought.
sentences.i: his five companions laid hands on Jamuqa, seized him, and brought him to Chinggis Qahan.
sentences.n: in-ü is the third-person genitive set after its noun (Ming 他的): “companions of his”. The “his” can only be Jamuqa’s, and the next units say so outright (nököd-teġen). γardažu is γar “hand” + -da- “lay a hand on” + -žu, and barižu is bari- “seize”: two converbs and a finite verb, abčiražuγ̇u. That verb is Ming 將着來, “bring along”; I read it as ab- “take” + a form of ire- “come” (a compound meaning “bring”), which is an analysis rather than a certainty. Čiṅgis is glossed 太祖 by the Ming, which treats it as a name.

sentences.t: Žamuqa nököd-teġen barižu iregdežü Qaγan anda-da ügüle.

morph.gloss: dative-locative: to, by [伴當每(自的)行]
reflexive-possessive: one’s own [伴當每(自的)行]
sworn brother, pledged friend [契合 行]
to speak, say (bare stem, here a plain ‘said’) [說]

sentences.l: Jamuqa companions-his-own-by seized, brought-being, Qaγan anda-to spoke.
sentences.i: Jamuqa, seized by his own companions and brought, said to the Qahan, his sworn brother:
sentences.n: A passive: iregdežü is ire- “come” + the passive -gde- + -žü (Ming 被來着), “being brought”; the agent is nököd-teġen, the dative-locative standing for “by” (Ming 伴當每(自的)行). Qaγan anda-da is “to the Qahan, the sworn brother”: anda is the pledged brother, and Jamuqa will use the word again in his plea below. ügüle is the bare stem, which I render “said”; in other places the bare stem is a command, and here it is plainly narrative.

sentences.t: "Qara keriġe qaramba noγosu bariqu bolba.

morph.gloss: a kind of duck (Ming 黑鴨名 ‘black duck’; form unanalysed) [黑鴨名]

sentences.l: Black crow, qaramba duck, seizing became.
sentences.i: “A black crow has come to seize a qaramba duck.
sentences.n: Jamuqa’s speech opens (Shiratori prints the opening mark at Qara) with a riddling figure. I give the words as they come. qaramba is the Ming 黑鴨名, a kind of duck; whether it is one bird (“a qaramba duck”) or the crow’s own name I cannot tell. bariqu bolba is bari- “seize” + the participle -qu + bolba “became”, “came to be seizing”; none of the nouns carries a case ending, so which seizes which rests on word order alone (the first is the seizer, as in the lines below, where the sense is plain). The following lines repeat the pattern bariqu bolba with two more birds and then with slaves taking their lord, so I read all three as one figure of seizing; what the birds stand for the Ming does not say.

sentences.t: Qaraču boγ̇ol Qān-dur(i)-jan γar kürgekü bolba.

morph.gloss: ruler, sovereign, khan (the short form beside qaγan) [皇帝 自的行]
dative-locative: to (back-vowel form) [皇帝 自的行]
reflexive-possessive: one’s own (the (i) is Shiratori’s) [皇帝 自的行]
to bring to reach, to lay on (causative of kür- ‘reach’) [到的]

sentences.l: Commoner slave own-Qan-to hand reaching became.
sentences.i: A commoner, a slave, has laid his hand on his own Qan.
sentences.n: Qaraču is “commoner” (Ming 丁民, “commoners”; an earlier part has 下民 “lowly people” and analyses it as qara “black” + -ču). Qaraču boγ̇ol could also be a pair, “commoners and slaves”; I take it as apposition, as the list below gives boγ̇ol separately. Qān-dur(i)-jan is Qān + -dur + the reflexive -jan, “to his own Qan”, with Shiratori’s (i). γar kürgekü is “hand + reaching”: kürge- is kür- “reach” in a causative (“bring to reach”), so “to lay a hand on”, as with γarda- above.

sentences.t: Qaγan anda min-u jaγ̇u egdekü

morph.gloss: to err, be at fault (Ming 差; stem inferred) [差的]

sentences.l: Qaγan anda, my what faulty?
sentences.i: Qahan, my sworn brother, what fault is mine?
sentences.n: min-u is the genitive of bi “I”, set after its noun in the Mongol but before it in English. egdekü is the Ming 差, “to err, be at fault, go amiss” (egde-, stem inferred) + the participle -kü, and jaγ̇u is “what” (Ming 怎, which would be “how”): “how/what is erring of mine?”. This line returns word for word at the end of the speech, with Boγda for Qaγan. Shiratori prints no question mark and the Mongol has no interrogative particle, so the question is carried by jaγ̇u alone.

sentences.t: boro-quladu borčin-sono bariqu bolba.

morph.gloss: a kind of bird (Ming 鳥名); boro may be ‘grey’, not confirmed [鳥名]
a kind of duck (Ming 鴨名); form unanalysed [鴨名]

sentences.l: Boro-quladu, borčin-sono, seizing became.
sentences.i: A boro-quladu bird has come to seize a borčin-sono duck.
sentences.n: Two more bird names, each given by the Ming as the name of a bird (鳥名) or duck (鴨名): boro-quladu and borčin-sono. I leave both unanalysed; boro may be “grey” but the Ming does not say so. The pattern bariqu bolba is the same as in the first line of the speech, and the two lines go with the first pair, one bird seizing another.

sentences.t: Boγ̇ol nekün budun ežen(i)-jen böšöžü nemdežü bariqu bolba.

morph.gloss: common people, the mass (Ming 本 ‘own’; sense uncertain) [本]
reflexive-possessive: one’s own (front-vowel form; the (i) is Shiratori’s) [主 自的行]
to surround (stem inferred from the Ming 圍) [圍着]
to plot secretly (stem inferred from the Ming 潛謀) [潛謀着]

sentences.l: Slave, household-people, commons, own-lord-(object) surrounding, plotting, seizing became.
sentences.i: Slaves, household servants and the common folk have surrounded their own lord, plotted against him, and seized him.
sentences.n: Boγ̇ol nekün budun is a list of three kinds of subordinate: slaves, household people (Ming (家)人) and budun, which the Ming glosses 本 (“own, proper”). I read budun as “the common run” by the sense, since “own” makes no sense beside ežen-jen “their own lord”; this is a doubt. ežen(i)-jen is ežen “lord” + the reflexive -jen, “their own lord”, the (i) being Shiratori’s (the Ming 主 自的行). böšöžü is Ming 圍着 “surrounding” and nemdežü Ming 潛謀着 “plotting secretly”; the stems böšö- and nemde- are inferred from those glosses alone. The chain ends, as before, in bariqu bolba.

sentences.t: Boγda anda min-u jaγ̇u egdekü" keġen ügüleġesü

morph.gloss: wise, holy, sage (Ming 賢明) [賢明]
to err, be at fault (Ming 差; stem inferred) [差的]
conditional converb: if, when (front-vowel form) [說呵]

sentences.l: Wise anda, my what faulty? saying, speaking-when,
sentences.i: Wise sworn brother, what fault is mine?” When he had said this,
sentences.n: The speech closes with the refrain, now with Boγda (Ming 賢明, “wise, holy”) in place of Qaγan; I take it as an epithet, not a name, since the Ming glosses it as an adjective. Shiratori puts the closing mark after egdekü. ügüleġesü is ügüle- “say” + the conditional -ġesü (front-vowel form of -γasu): “when (he) said”, with the quotation closed by keġen “saying”. The subject, Jamuqa, is understood.

sentences.t: Žamuqa-jin tere üge-dür Čiṅgis Qaγan žarliγ bolurun:

morph.gloss: Jamuqa, a man's name [人名 的]
genitive: of (after a vowel) [人名 的]
dative-locative: in, at (front-vowel form) [言語 裏]
Chinggis, the title borne by Temüjin from 1206 [太祖︀]

sentences.l: Jamuqa’s that word-in Chinggis Qaγan decree making-when:
sentences.i: At those words of Jamuqa, Chinggis Qahan issued a decree:
sentences.n: Žamuqa-jin tere üge-dür is “in that word of Jamuqa’s”, the genitive before the noun, with tere (“that”) between, then the dative-locative -dür; the sense is “at/by those words”. žarliγ bolurun, “decree, when making”, is the formula that introduces a decree (see the same words in the preceding parts). The decree that follows has a doubled form; each half begins with Tus.

sentences.t: "Tus Qān-dur(i)-jan γar kürgegsen küġün-i ker aγ̇uldaqu.

morph.gloss: own, proper, rightful (tus qān ‘one’s own true lord’) [正主]
ruler, sovereign, khan (the short form beside qaγan) [皇帝 自的行]
dative-locative: to (back-vowel form) [皇帝 自的行]
reflexive-possessive: one’s own (the (i) is Shiratori’s) [皇帝 自的行]
to bring to reach, to lay on (causative of kür-) [到了的]
past participle: who has …-ed (front-vowel form) [到了的]
to let remain, spare (stem inferred from the Ming 敎存) [敎存的]

sentences.l: Rightful own-Qan-to hand laid person-(object) how to be spared?
sentences.i: “How is a man who has laid his hand on his own rightful lord to be spared?
sentences.n: Shiratori opens the quotation at Tus. tus (Ming 正主) is “own, rightful”: tus Qān, “one’s true lord”. kürgegsen is kürge- + -gsen, “who has laid (a hand)”, a past participle; küġün-i is “person” in the accusative. aγ̇uldaqu is the Ming 敎存 “cause to remain”, hence “let live, spare”; the stem aγ̇ulda- is inferred from the gloss. The sentence is a rhetorical question carried by ker “how”, and is the first of two parallel sentences, one on the traitor and one on his kin.

sentences.t: Teimün küġün ken-dür nököčekü.

morph.gloss: such, of that kind (related to tein ‘thus’) [那般每]
to be a companion (from nökör) [做得伴]

sentences.l: Such man whom-to companion-be?
sentences.i: Such a man: to whom could he be a companion?
sentences.n: Teimün is “such, of that kind” (Ming 那般每). nököčekü is nököče- “be a companion” (from nökör) + the participle -kü, and ken-dür is “to whom”. Rhetorical: no one would have him.

sentences.t: Tus Qān-dur(i)-jan γar kürgegsed haran-i uruγ-a an-u kürtele mököriġülüdkün"

morph.gloss: ruler, sovereign, khan (the short form beside qaγan) [皇帝 自的行]
dative-locative: to (back-vowel form) [皇帝 自的行]
reflexive-possessive: one’s own (the (i) is Shiratori’s) [皇帝 自的行]
to bring to reach, to lay on [到了的每]
their, his (third-person genitive, back-vowel form, set after its noun) [他的]
terminal converb: until, up to [直到]

words.reading: 抹闊舌里兀魯惕坤 mököriġülüdkün

morph.gloss: to cut down, behead (Ming 處斬) [處斬]
ending of the plural polite command: you (all) … [處斬]

sentences.l: Rightful own-Qan-to hand laid people-(object), kin-to their until, let-them-be-beheaded
sentences.i: Those who have laid hands on their own rightful lord, the men, down to their very kin: let them be beheaded!”
sentences.n: The second half. kürgegsed is the plural of the participle (-d), “those who have laid”; haran-i is haran “common people” + the accusative; uruγ-a is uruγ “offspring, kin” with the dative-locative -a (Ming 行), and an-u kürtele is “their … until, as far as” (kür- “reach” + -tele), so “down to their kin”. I read the whole as “even their kin included”; the exact function of uruγ-a is not clear to me. mököriġülüdkün is mököri- “behead” (Ming 處斬) + the causative -ġül- + -dkün, an ending glossed in earlier parts as a plural polite command: “let (you all) have them beheaded”. So the decree is addressed to executioners as an order. The quotation opened at Tus closes after mököriġülüdkün.

sentences.t: keġen žarliγ bolba.
sentences.l: saying decree made.
sentences.i: Thus he made the decree.
sentences.n: keġen (“saying”) closes the quotation, and žarliγ bolba is “decree became”, i.e. he made the decree.

sentences.t: Mün Žamuqa-jin ile ima-ji γardaγsan haran-i mököriġülžü ögbe.

morph.gloss: Jamuqa, a man's name [人名 的]
genitive: of (after a vowel) [人名 的]
openly, face to face, in the open [對面]
him, that one (oblique stem of the 3rd-person pronoun; form unclear) [他行]
to lay a hand on, set hand to [下手的]

sentences.l: Just Jamuqa’s face-to-face him-(object) hand-laid people-(object) beheading-caused gave.
sentences.i: And in Jamuqa’s very presence he had the men who had laid hands on him beheaded and gave them up.
sentences.n: Mün Žamuqa-jin ile is “Jamuqa’s very … face to face”: ile is the Ming 對面 “facing”, so “in Jamuqa’s presence”. ima-ji is the accusative of the third-person pronoun and points back to Jamuqa, so γardaγsan haran-i is “the men who laid hands on him”, the five companions. mököriġülžü is the causative “had beheaded” + -žü; ögbe is ög- “give” + -be, “gave”. What was given, and to whom, is not said. I read ögbe as “he gave (them up)” and flag it.

sentences.t: Čiṅgis Qaγan Žamuqa-da ügüle keġen ügülerün:

morph.gloss: Chinggis, the title borne by Temüjin from 1206 [太祖︀]
Jamuqa, a man's name [人名 行]
to speak, say (bare stem, here a plain ‘said’) [說]

sentences.l: Chinggis Qaγan Jamuqa-to spoke, saying, speaking-when:
sentences.i: Chinggis Qahan spoke to Jamuqa, saying:
sentences.n: A tight redundancy: ügüle keġen ügülerün, “spoke, saying, while speaking”, the usual way of introducing a quotation. Žamuqa-da carries the dative -da (back-vowel form).

sentences.t: "Edöġe bida. qojar qamtudba; nököčeje.

morph.gloss: to be joined, to come together (from qamtu ‘together’; stem inferred from the Ming 相合) [相合下]
to be a companion (from nökör) [做伴咱]
hortative, first person plural: let us (front-vowel form) [做伴咱]

sentences.l: “Now we two together have become; let us be companions.
sentences.i: “Now the two of us have come together; let us be companions.
sentences.n: Quotation opens at Edöġe. bida is inclusive “we”; qojar “two”. qamtudba is qamtu “together” turned into a verb (qamtud-, stem inferred from the Ming 相合) + -ba past, “have joined”. nököčeje is nököče- “be a companion” + the first-person hortative -je (Ming 咱: the Ming ‘us’). Shiratori prints a full stop after bida and a semicolon after qamtudba; I keep the sentence whole and follow his semicolon.

sentences.t: Öreġele kilγun bolulčažu aγ̇asu öġermičilen qaγačan sedkimü či.

morph.gloss: one (of a pair), a single (Ming 一隻); form unanalysed [一隻]
to do together (bol- “become” with a reciprocal; stem inferred, as in the glossary) [共做着]
to be, to live, to pass (time) [過呵]
conditional converb: if, when (back-vowel form) [過呵]
to make oneself apart, act separately (from öġere ‘other’; stem inferred) [別做]

sentences.l: One shaft together making, if we pass, separately-making, parting, think you.
sentences.i: If we are to pass our lives as a single cart-shaft, you think of going your own way and parting.
sentences.n: The hardest sentence in the part, and I give it with doubts. Öreġele is the Ming 一隻 “one (of a pair)”; kilγun the Ming 車轅 “cart-shaft”: the figure of two companions pulling as one shaft (compare kilgün, “shaft”, in earlier parts). bolulčažu is bol- “become” + -ulča- “together” + -žu; aγ̇asu is a- “be, pass (time)” + the conditional -γ̇asu, so “if we pass”. öġermičilen is Ming 別做, “making oneself apart”, built on öġere “other, apart” (the verb stem is inferred); qaγačan is “parting”; sedkimü is sedki- “think” + the present -mü; and či “you” stands last. I read the conditional as the frame and the last three words as the charge. Whether the sentence is a reproach (“and yet you think of leaving”) or a flat statement I cannot settle from the grammar. Shiratori puts the full stop after či.

sentences.t: Edöġe nigen-e qamtu ažu umartaγsan(i)-jan duradγaldužu untaraγsan(i)-jan seriġülülečežü aja.

words.reading: 兀馬舌兒塔黑撒你-顏 umartaγsan(i)-jan

morph.gloss: to forget (Ming 忘) [忘了的 自的行]
past participle: what has been …-ed [忘了的 自的行]
reflexive-possessive: one’s own (the (i) is Shiratori’s) [忘了的 自的行]

words.reading: 都︀舌剌惕中合勒都︀周 duradγaldužu

morph.gloss: to remind, bring up, mention (stem uncertain, as in the glossary; Ming 提說) [共提說 着]
reciprocal: one another [共提說 着]

words.reading: 穩榻舌剌黑撒你-顏 untaraγsan(i)-jan

morph.gloss: to sleep [睡着的 自的行]
past participle: that has …-ed (here “one who has slept”) [睡着的 自的行]
reflexive-possessive: one’s own (the (i) is Shiratori’s) [睡着的 自的行]

words.reading: 薛舌里兀魯勒扯周 seriġülülečežü

morph.gloss: to be aware, to wake (variant spelling of sere- in sereġülžü below; stem inferred from the Ming 覺省) [共覺省着]
to be, to live, to pass (time) [過咱]
hortative, first person plural: let us (back-vowel form) [過咱]

sentences.l: Now in one place together dwelling, forgotten-own reminding-one-another, slept-own waking-one-another, let us pass.
sentences.i: Now let us live together in one place, reminding each other of what each has forgotten and waking each other from sleep.
sentences.n: A reciprocal chain. umartaγsan(i)-jan is umarta- “forget” + the participle -γsan + the reflexive, “what one has forgotten” (Ming 忘了的 自的行); untaraγsan(i)-jan is the same for untara- “sleep” (Ming 睡着的). duradγaldužu is duradγa- “remind, bring up” (as in the earlier duradγarun) + -ldu- (the reciprocal, as in alalduqui) + -žu; seriġülülečežü is seri- “be aware” + the causative -ġülü- + -lče- “together” + -žü. The whole reads “reminding one another … rousing one another” (Ming 共提說, 共覺省). The stems duradγa- and seri- are inferred from the Ming. aja is a- “pass” + -ja “let us”, the hortative as in nököče-je; the same word “a-” as ažu, “dwelling”.

sentences.t: Öġere ber aṅgida jabuγ̇asu ölžetü qutuγtu anda min-u büleġe.

morph.gloss: conditional converb: if, when (back-vowel form) [行呵]
blessing, good fortune [吉慶 有的]
possessive: having, with [吉慶 有的]
past narrative: there was, used to be (front-vowel form) [有來]

sentences.l: Apart also outside if going, fortunate blessed anda my was.
sentences.i: Even when we went our separate ways apart, you were my fortunate, blessed sworn brother.
sentences.n: öġere ber aṅgida is three small words in a row: “other/apart, even, outside”. jabuγ̇asu is jabu- “go, walk” + the conditional, “if/when going”. ölžetü is ölže “good fortune” + -tü “having” (Ming 吉慶) and qutuγtu is qutuγ “blessing” + -tu “having” (Ming 吉慶 有的): both are the possessive pattern, “fortune-having, blessing-having”. büleġe is the narrative past of bü- “to be”: “there was, you were”. No pronoun is expressed; the addressee is Jamuqa, the “sworn brother of mine”.

sentences.t: Ünen üküldüküi üdür öre žürüge-ben ebedkü büleġe či.

morph.gloss: to die (stem inferred from the Ming 捨死) [共捨死的]
reciprocal: one another, together (front-vowel form) [共捨死的]
hollow of the heart, breast (Ming 心窩) [心窩]
reflexive-possessive: one’s own (front-vowel form, after a vowel) [心 自的行]
to ache, hurt (stem inferred from the Ming 痛) [痛的]
past narrative: there was, used to be (front-vowel form) [有來]

sentences.l: Truly dying-together day bosom heart-own aching was you.
sentences.i: In truth, on the day of our dying together, your own heart ached in your breast, you.
sentences.n: Ünen is “true, truly” (Ming 實). üküldüküi is ükü- “die” + the reciprocal -ldü- + the participle -küi, “dying together” (Ming 共捨死的). öre is the Ming 心窩, “the hollow of the heart, the breast” (not the “heart, mind” of earlier parts: the Ming adds 窩), and žürüge-ben is “heart” + the reflexive -ben, “one’s own heart” (Ming 心 自的行). ebedkü is ebed- “ache, hurt” (stem inferred from 痛) + -kü, and büleġe, as before, “was”. The reflexive -ben on žürüge I take as a possessive, “your own heart”; the Ming has 心 自的行 with no “in”. The unit ends with či “you”, set off by its own full stop. This is the second of three sentence-final či in the speech (after sedkimü či above, and before the next unit); I take it as an emphatic address to Jamuqa and note the pattern.

sentences.t: Aṅgida ber öġere jabuγ̇asu alalduqui üdür aγ̇ušigi žürüge-ben ebedkü büleġe. či.

morph.gloss: conditional converb: if, when (back-vowel form) [行呵]
reflexive-possessive: one’s own (front-vowel form, after a vowel) [心 自的行]
to ache, hurt (stem inferred from the Ming 痛) [痛的]
past narrative: there was, used to be (front-vowel form) [有來]

sentences.l: Outside also apart if going, mutual-killing day lungs heart-own aching was. you.
sentences.i: And even when we went apart, on the day we fought one another, your own heart ached in your lungs, you.
sentences.n: This line mirrors the one before: “the day of dying together” becomes “the day of killing one another”. alalduqui is ala- “kill” + -ldu- + the participle -qui, “killing each other” (Ming 厮殺︀的). aγ̇ušigi is the Ming 肺 “lung(s)”; I leave the final -gi unanalysed. It stands where öre stood in the line before, so I read it as the place of the aching (“in your lungs”); “your heart and lungs” is the other possibility and the bare words do not exclude it. Again či stands apart after büleġe and its full stop: the third sentence-final či (compare 150 and 176), an emphatic “you”.

sentences.t: Keli kēġesü Kereid irgen-lüġe Qalaqalžid-Eled-te qadqulduqui-dur

morph.gloss: when, at any time (Ming 幾時; uncertain) [幾時]
conditional: if one says (written kēġesü) [說呵]
comitative: with (front-vowel form) [百姓 一同]

words.reading: 中合剌中合勒只惕-額列惕-帖 Qalaqalžid-Eled-te

glyphs.s: 中合剌中合勒只惕-額列惕-帖

words.reading: 中合惕中忽勒都︀中灰-突︀舌兒 qadqulduqui-dur

glyphs.s: 中合惕中忽勒都︀中灰-突︀舌兒

morph.gloss: to fight (stem inferred from the Ming 厮殺) [厮殺︀的 時]
reciprocal: one another [厮殺︀的 時]
dative-locative: at the time of [厮殺︀的 時]

sentences.l: When saying, the Kereid people with, Qalaqalžid-Eled-at fighting-at,
sentences.i: As to when: at the time of fighting with the Kereid people at Qalaqaljid-Eled,
sentences.n: Keli kēġesü is “when, if one says” (Ming 幾時 說呵): an imagined question, “when?”, which the clauses below answer; kēġesü is keġe- “say” + -sü, written with a long ē. irgen-lüġe is “with the people”, the comitative in its front-vowel form. Qalaqalžid-Eled-te is a place (Ming 地名行); I do not split it (Eled is probably “sands”, as an earlier part reads el + -d) and give it with the dative-locative -te. qadqulduqui-dur is qadqul- “fight” (stem inferred from the Ming 厮殺) + the reciprocal -ldu- + -qui + -dur, “at the time of fighting each other”.

sentences.t: Waṅ-Qān ečige-de ügülegsed üges(i)-jen sereġülžü ilegsen tusa čin-u bi-že.

morph.gloss: Wang Qan, ruler of the Kereid [人名]
past participle, plural: those who/what …-ed [說了的(每)]
reflexive-possessive: one’s own (front-vowel form; the (i) is Shiratori’s) [言語(每)自的行]
to be aware, to remember (stem inferred from the Ming 省) [提省着]
stem-final n before a case ending [你的]

sentences.l: Wang Qan father-to said words-own reminding sent, benefit your is.
sentences.i: Your service was this: reminding Father Wang Qan of the words spoken to him, you sent word.
sentences.n: ečige-de is “to Father” with -de, and Waṅ-Qān ečige is “Father Wang Qan”, the title the conventions give for Qān ečige. ügülegsed üges(i)-jen is “the words (plural: üge + -s, with Shiratori’s (i) before the reflexive) spoken … their own words”; ügülegsed is the plural participle ügüle- + -gsed, “those said”. sereġülžü is sere- “be aware” + the causative, “causing to remember” (Ming 提省着); ilegsen is ile- “send” + the participle (Ming 敎來的, here the earlier sense of “sent word”). tusa čin-u bi-že is “your benefit/service there is indeed”: čin-u is the genitive of či, and bi-že is bü- (as bi- before -že) + the assertive particle. Who spoke the words, and whose service this is, the grammar leaves open: ügülegsed is a plural participle, “those who spoke”, with no named speakers. I read the clause as the first of two services Chinggis credits to Jamuqa, and so give it as a reminder to Wang Qan; that reading is uncertain. The object of ilegsen is not given here; the last unit makes it kele, “word”.

sentences.t: Basa Naiman irgen-i üge-ġer üküġülžü ama-γ̇ar alažu

morph.gloss: accusative: marks the object [百姓 行]
to die (stem inferred from the Ming 死) [敎死着]

sentences.l: Again Naiman people-(object) word-by killing-caused, mouth-by killing,
sentences.i: And again, you had the Naiman people put to death by words, you killed them by mouth,
sentences.n: The last long sentence is hard, and this stretch most of all. Basa is “again”; Naiman irgen-i is the Naiman people with the accusative. üge-ġer is üge “word” + the instrumental -ġer (front-vowel form): “by word”, and ama-γ̇ar is ama “mouth” + -γ̇ar (back-vowel form): “by mouth”; the Ming glosses 言語裏 and 口敎 as “by speech” and “by mouth-order”. üküġülžü is ükü- “die” + the causative -ġül- + -žü (Ming 敎死着): “causing to die”. alažu is “killing”. The sense, that Jamuqa had the Naiman killed through a word of his, I cannot confirm; I only give the grammar, and the English is a literal rendering, not a settled meaning.

sentences.t: ajuγ̇uluγsan(i)-jan adalidγatuγai keġežü

words.reading: 阿余兀魯黑撒你-顏 ajuγ̇uluγsan(i)-jan

morph.gloss: to fear (stem inferred from the Ming 怕) [敎怕來的]
past participle: that has …-ed [敎怕來的]
reflexive-possessive: one’s own (the (i) is Shiratori’s) [敎怕來的]

words.reading: 阿荅里惕中合禿中孩 adalidγatuγai

morph.gloss: to liken, set as an example (adali “alike” made into a verb; stem inferred from the Ming 比方) [敎比方者︀]
optative: let it be … [敎比方者︀]

sentences.l: fear-caused-own let-be-compared saying,
sentences.i: and saying, ‘Let those I have frightened be an example,’
sentences.n: ajuγ̇uluγsan(i)-jan is aju- “fear” + the causative -γ̇ul- + -γsan + the reflexive (Ming 敎怕來的 自的行): “the ones one has frightened”, with Shiratori’s (i). adalidγatuγai is adalidγa- (adali “alike” made into a verb) + the optative -tuγai: “let (it) be made alike, compared”; the Ming 敎比方者 reads “let it be an example”. keġežü is keġe- “say” + -žü. The reflexive -jan points to the subject of keġežü, so inside the quoted words the speaker is “I”; the reading of this clause as a warning to those frightened is a guess from the Ming. The reflexive -jan may refer to the Naiman or to someone else; the grammar does not decide.

sentences.t: kele ilegsen čin-u tusa bolžuγ̇ui-že" keġen

morph.gloss: stem-final n before a case ending [你的]
to become [做了有來 也者︀]
past narrative (back-vowel form) [做了有來 也者︀]
assertion particle: indeed, surely [做了有來 也者︀]

sentences.l: word sent, your benefit become indeed, saying.
sentences.i: you sent word. The service was indeed yours,” he said.
sentences.n: kele ilegsen is “word that was sent”, the same ilegsen as above; čin-u tusa is “your benefit”; bolžuγ̇ui-že is bol- “become” + the narrative past -žuγ̇ui + the assertive -že, “has indeed become”, answering bi-že above. Shiratori closes the long quotation after -že, and keġen “saying” follows. Chinggis’s speech thus names two services, one at the Kereid battle and one concerning the Naiman; the second is the harder to read, as the notes above say.
